story: Proclamation 11055 puts 100 percent tariffs on imported thermal drones and docking stations, the exact hardware Alaska bought for its roadless villages, and Alaska bought American

claims.claim: Proclamation 11055 is titled "Adjusting Imports of Unmanned Aircraft Systems and Unmanned Aircraft Systems Components Into the United States".
claims.verbatim: Proclamation 11055--Adjusting Imports of Unmanned Aircraft Systems and Unmanned Aircraft Systems Components Into the United States
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: Title confirmed identically on the Federal Register API record for document 2026-16979 and on the FR full text HTML. The word Imports is in the title itself, which is load bearing for the deck's argument.

claims.claim: The proclamation was signed on August 13th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this thirteenth day of August, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: Signature block gives the date in words. Federal Register API metadata separately carries signing_date 2026-08-13. This date anchors every 180 day calculation in the document.

claims.claim: The proclamation was published in the Federal Register on August 19th, 2026 at citation 91 FR 53699.
claims.verbatim: Citation: 91 FR 53699
claims.source_outlet: Federal Register, Office of the Federal Register API
claims.note: Metadata record for document number 2026-16979. Six days between signing and publication.

claims.claim: The proclamation imposes a 100 percent ad valorem duty rate on the import of the uncrewed aircraft systems identified in Annex I.
claims.verbatim: Specifically, I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to impose a 100 percent ad valorem duty rate on the import of UAS
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: The phrase is on the import of UAS, not on UAS. Do not cite a clause number, the paragraph numbering was not cleanly resolvable across renderings.

claims.claim: The 100 percent rate applies to uncrewed aircraft systems with a maximum take off weight of more than 25 kilograms.
claims.verbatim: UAS with a maximum take-off weight of more than 25 kilograms
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: First of three named categories in the 100 percent sentence.

claims.claim: The 100 percent rate applies as its own separate category to uncrewed aircraft systems that integrate thermal imagers, with no weight condition attached.
claims.verbatim: UAS that integrate thermal imagers
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: The category is listed in series after the weight category and is not qualified by weight, so on the face of the text an imported small thermal drone falls in the 100 percent band rather than the 25 percent band. The proclamation does not spell out that consequence. Actual scope is set by the Annex I HTS lines, which were not retrieved. Present as what the text says, never as an agency ruling.

claims.claim: The 100 percent rate applies as its own separate category to uncrewed aircraft system docking stations.
claims.verbatim: UAS docking stations
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: Third named category, listed independently of the aircraft categories.

claims.claim: The proclamation sets a 25 percent ad valorem duty rate on imports of uncrewed aircraft systems with a maximum take off weight of 25 kilograms or less.
claims.verbatim: 25 percent ad valorem duty rate on imports of UAS with a maximum take-off weight of 25 kilograms or less
claims.note: The Annex II band. The operative word is again imports.

claims.claim: The first tranche of duties takes effect at 12:01 a.m. eastern time on September 3rd, 2026.
claims.verbatim: on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on September 3, 2026
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: Covers both the 100 percent Annex I products and the 25 percent Annex II products. Confirmed on both the govinfo and Federal Register renderings.

claims.claim: The duty attaches only to goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, which is customs language for imported merchandise clearing the border.
claims.verbatim: Effective with respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on September 3, 2026
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: The structural claim the deck rests on, verified as text. The trigger is an import event. The deck must not say the proclamation exempts domestic manufacturers, because it grants no exemption, it simply never reaches them. A domestically assembled aircraft can still contain imported components, which is what the second tranche is about.

claims.claim: A second tranche sets a 25 percent ad valorem duty on the uncrewed aircraft system components listed in Annex III.
claims.verbatim: for the UAS components listed in Annex III to this proclamation, the applicable ad valorem duty rate imposed pursuant to section 232 shall be 25 percent
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: The components rate is 25 percent, not 100 percent.

claims.claim: The Annex III components duty takes effect at 12:01 a.m. eastern time on February 9th, 2027.
claims.verbatim: on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on February 9, 2027, for the UAS components listed in Annex III to this proclamation
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: The components clause states a literal calendar date, not a relative period.

claims.claim: The delay applies to companies on the Department of War Blue UAS Cleared List, the Blue UAS Framework, or the FCC Conditional Approval List on September 2nd, 2026.
claims.verbatim: For companies on the DoW's Blue UAS Cleared List, the Blue UAS Framework, or the FCC's Conditional Approval List on September 2, 2026
claims.note: The qualifying date is the day before the first tranche bites. Three lists qualify, not one. Relief is limited to the listed products and their components, so it is product scoped in effect.

claims.claim: For those listed companies the first tranche effective date is pushed to 180 days from the date of the proclamation.
claims.verbatim: the effective date referenced in clause (1) of this proclamation shall be 180 days from the date of this proclamation
claims.note: The 180 days runs from the date of the proclamation, August 13th 2026, and not from September 2nd and not from publication. 180 days after August 13th 2026 is February 9th 2027, which matches the literal Annex III date in C12 exactly. The two deadlines converge on the same day by construction. Never quote this clause as if it prints February 9th, because it does not.

claims.claim: The duty rate is capped at no higher than 15 percent for products of Japan, the Republic of Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, or a member nation of the European Union when critical component origin is certified.
claims.verbatim: For products of Japan, the Republic of Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, or a member nation of the European Union, the duty rate shall be no higher than 15 percent
claims.note: Conditional on importer certification that substantially all the critical components and technology are products of the allied set including the United States and the United Kingdom. Do not print the cap without the condition.

claims.claim: The duty rate is capped at no higher than 10 percent for products of the United Kingdom under the same certification condition.
claims.verbatim: For products of the United Kingdom, the duty rate shall be no higher than 10 percent
claims.note: The single lowest cap in the proclamation, five points below the allied group.

claims.claim: The proclamation is issued under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended.
claims.verbatim: section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, [19 U.S.C. 1862]
claims.note: Section 232 is the national security adjustment of imports authority, an import authority by its own terms. Also cited are section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974 and section 301 of title 3 United States Code. Do not assert a legal conclusion beyond that.

claims.claim: The words Alaska, rural, public safety and firefighting do not appear anywhere in the proclamation.
claims.verbatim: Alaska: DOES NOT APPEAR
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: Negative finding, tested independently against both the govinfo rendering and the Federal Register full text HTML, both returning absent. A negative has no quote. Phrase as the proclamation never mentions Alaska, never as a claim about intent.

claims.claim: The proclamation names search and rescue once, in a sentence listing what federal agencies use uncrewed aircraft systems for.
claims.verbatim: UAS are used by many executive departments and agencies (agencies) for purposes of law enforcement, scientific research, environmental monitoring, aerial mapping, surveillance, agriculture, disaster relief, and search and rescue.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, Federal Register
claims.note: A recital about federal agency use, not a carve out and not a finding about state or local responders. Do not imply the proclamation protects search and rescue operators.

claims.claim: A 12.4 million dollar federal grant started an Alaska initiative to use advanced drones to fly long distances.
claims.verbatim: A $12.4 million federal grant kick-starts an initiative to use advanced drones to fly long distances.
claims.note: Background, published January 17th 2025, outside the run window. Single secondary source for the dollar figure, so attribute it to the outlet.

claims.claim: The Alaska drone initiative funded by that grant is called Scalable Operations and Advanced Remote Technologies, or SOAR.
claims.verbatim: the $12.4 million Scalable Operations and Advanced Remote Technologies (SOAR) initiative
claims.note: SOAR is the initiative and SMART is the funding program. The article says it is funded through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 as part of the Strengthening Mobility and Revolutionizing Transportation program. Do not collapse the two.

claims.claim: Twenty two drones were already stationed in Alaska before the second phase of the program.
claims.verbatim: That's in addition to twenty-two already stationed in Alaska.
claims.note: Figure is as of January 2025 and may have moved. Hedge as of early 2025.

claims.claim: The second phase is to place fifty drones and docking stations across two states, fifteen in California and thirty five in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: In this second phase, fifty drones and docking stations will dot the two states, fifteen in California and thirty-five in Alaska.
claims.note: Fifteen plus thirty five is fifty, arithmetic consistent. The source is future tense, will dot, so present as planned and not delivered.

claims.claim: The aircraft used in phase one of the Alaska program were US made Skydio X10 drones, used for purposes including search and rescue.
claims.verbatim: The US-made Skydio X10 drones in Phase 1 were used for various purposes, from assisting with search and rescue missions to capturing real-time conditions in emergencies.
claims.note: The outlet itself writes US-made, which independently corroborates the manufacturer statement in C32. Scoped to Phase 1 only. No source confirms which airframe phase two buys.

claims.claim: The grant funding supplies drones, docking stations and Starlink connections to communities around Alaska, and trains drone operators.
claims.verbatim: The funding will be used to train drone operators and supply drones, docking stations, and Starlink connections to various communities around the state.
claims.note: This sentence is what puts docking stations, one of the three 100 percent categories, squarely inside the Alaska purchase.

claims.claim: A separate 1.13 million dollar SMART grant covers the Seward Highway corridor.
claims.verbatim: Meanwhile on the Seward Highway, a $1.13 million SMART grant will give travelers a little peace of mind as they move along the corridor, bounded by mountains and ocean.
claims.note: This is the award the article calls a SMART grant in those words, unlike the 12.4 million dollar one.

claims.claim: Alaska DOT and PF Commissioner Ryan Anderson said improving safety for Alaskans in rural and remote areas is part of the department's mission.
claims.verbatim: Improving safety for Alaskans living and traveling in rural and remote areas of our state is part of Alaska DOT&PF's mission
claims.note: Attributed in the article to DOT and PF Commissioner Ryan Anderson speaking about the SOAR initiative.

claims.claim: Alaska DOT and PF runs a drone program called the Alaska Rural Remote Operations Work Plan, or ARROW, funded through the US Department of Transportation SMART grant program.
claims.verbatim: Alaska Rural Remote Operations Work Plan (ARROW)
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities
claims.note: The department's own press release 24-0010. Background from April 2024. The release names the SMART grant program but carries no dollar figure. Nothing establishes that ARROW and SOAR are the same program, so keep them as two named things.

claims.claim: The program covers a 300 mile Kuskokwim ice road serving the Yukon Kuskokwim region around Bethel.
claims.verbatim: 300-mile Kuskokwim ice road
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities
claims.note: Primary. The 300 mile ice road is the concrete image of what roadless means here, a winter river highway between villages.

claims.claim: Alaska DOT and PF's Ryan Marlow said the technology adds crucial aerial support for search and rescue.
claims.verbatim: This technology is another tool in the toolbox for communities to document and respond to a rapidly changing environment, and add crucial aerial support for search and rescue
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities
claims.note: Primary. No verbatim job title was captured, so identify him as being with Alaska DOT and PF. Do not extend the quote past what is recorded here.

claims.claim: Clarence Daniel said the grant lets communities improve safe travel on trails for travelers going from one village to another during dangerous times of the year.
claims.verbatim: With this grant, we can improve safe travel on our trails for travelers from one village to another, which is important during dangerous times of the year.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities
claims.note: Primary. Affiliation was not verified, so attribute by name only and do not assign him to a village or tribal body.

claims.claim: Skydio states that the X10 is designed, assembled and supported in the U.S.
claims.value: Designed, assembled, and supported in the U.S.
claims.verbatim: Designed, assembled, and supported in the U.S. Prioritizes security from the start through trusted manufacturing partners, secure development practices, and more.
claims.note: The manufacturer's own statement about its own product, which is what it is and no more. It is marketing copy, not a customs origin ruling. The page is undated so date_of_source is the fetch date. Trusted manufacturing partners is not the same as saying every part is domestic, and that gap is where the February 9th components tranche lives. Frame as Skydio says, never as the X10 is exempt.

claims.claim: Skydio lists the X10 as weighing under 4.7 pounds, which is about 2.1 kilograms.
claims.verbatim: Weighing under 4.7 pounds
claims.note: 4.7 pounds is 2.13 kilograms, a derived conversion, far under the proclamation's 25 kilogram line. The page does not use the term maximum take off weight, so do not put the proclamation's phrase in Skydio's mouth.

claims.claim: Skydio offers radiometric thermal payloads for the X10, listed at 640 by 512 pixels.
claims.verbatim: radiometric thermal camera
claims.note: The payload names VT300-Z and VT300-L and the 640 by 512 figure were returned from the page but the strongest verbatim held is the shorter phrase, so hedge the resolution as listed at. This claim matters because it is what would put an X10 inside the proclamation's thermal imager category if such an aircraft were imported.

claims.claim: Skydio sells a docking station product called the Skydio Dock for X10.
claims.verbatim: Skydio Dock for X10
claims.note: The manufacturer's own product name. There is no source on where the dock itself is assembled, so the deck must not claim the dock is US made.

claims.claim: A thermal drone team joined the search for a missing hiker near Port Armstrong on Baranof Island, a search that ran August 11th to August 13th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: The search started up again Wednesday morning with help from the National Guard, Alaska Rescue Coordination Center, and a thermal drone team.
claims.note: In window and the strongest Alaska timing beat, since the search ran the same week the proclamation was signed on August 13th. The article says thermal, so the deck may say thermal. It does NOT name the drone operator or the aircraft, so the deck must not connect this team to DOT and PF, to SOAR, or to a Skydio X10. The search ran August 11th to 13th. Reported by Lauren Salemo.

claims.claim: Federal aviation rules define a small unmanned aircraft as one weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff including everything on board or attached.
claims.verbatim: Small unmanned aircraft means an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Government Publishing Office, 14 CFR Part 107
claims.note: Primary regulation text, definition at 14 CFR 107.3. 55 pounds is 24.95 kilograms, a derived conversion, which is why the proclamation's 25 kilogram line sits almost exactly on the FAA's small UAS ceiling. The correspondence is verified arithmetic. WHY the proclamation drew the line there is NOT established, so the deck may say the two thresholds coincide and must not say the proclamation adopted the FAA line.

killed.claim: The Skydio X10 or Skydio as a manufacturer appears on the Department of War Blue UAS Cleared List.
killed.why: UNVERIFIED, DO NOT PRINT. diu.mil/blue-uas-cleared-list no longer hosts the list and redirects to bluelist.dcma.mil, which returned HTTP 503 on two attempts. skydio.com/x10 does not contain the strings Blue UAS, NDAA or Section 848 at all. A Skydio blog URL for the listing returned 404. Since the proclamation's only carve out runs through that list, the deck must be written so it does not need this fact.

killed.claim: Alaska public safety agencies operate N imported DJI or other non US drones, the population actually exposed on September 3rd.
killed.why: No source found. Any number here would be invention. The deck should state plainly that the size of Alaska's imported drone fleet is not public rather than estimate it.

killed.claim: The Seward Highway avalanche program acronym AMAD stands for Avalanche Mitigation Alert Detection.
killed.why: The expansion was returned on a first pass but a targeted verbatim re-fetch did not reproduce it as a printed string. The 1.13 million dollar figure and the SMART attribution survive as C26.

killed.claim: The thirty five phase two Alaska aircraft are Skydio X10s.
killed.why: The Alaska Business Magazine sentence naming the X10 is explicitly scoped to Phase 1. No source states the phase two airframe.

killed.claim: The 12.4 million dollar award was a SMART grant.
killed.why: Rejected as phrased. The article names the initiative SOAR and describes it as funded through the SMART program. The award the article calls a SMART grant in those words is the separate 1.13 million dollar Seward Highway one. Kept in corrected form as C21.

killed.claim: The thermal drone team searching Port Armstrong was a DOT and PF or SOAR asset.
killed.why: The KCAW article names neither the operator nor the aircraft. Connecting it to the state program would be fabrication.

killed.claim: The proclamation exempts domestically manufactured aircraft.
killed.why: Rejected as framing. The proclamation grants no domestic exemption. Its duty is triggered by an import event, per C10, which is a different statement.
